props.title: Wild Things
props.initialSlug: Double-crosses and seduction in steamy Florida noir

sections.content: Wild Things (1998) epitomizes the late 90s neo-noir thriller explosion, combining sultry Florida atmosphere with labyrinthine plot twists. Director John McNaughton crafts a deliberately sleazy tale of sex, betrayal and murder that became infamous for its provocative marketing and shocking revelations. The film follows in the footsteps of Basic Instinct (1992) and Body Heat (1981), but adds an extra layer of complexity with its quadruple-cross narrative structure. Matt Dillon, Neve Campbell, and Denise Richards deliver performances that play with audience expectations, while Bill Murray provides crucial supporting work as a sleazy lawyer that hints at the film's underlying dark comedy.

sections.content: The legacy of Wild Things spawned a wave of direct-to-video sequels and similar erotic thrillers, but none captured the original's clever balance of exploitation and genuine narrative innovation. The film's infamous credits sequence reveals additional plot twists, a technique later borrowed by The Usual Suspects (1995) and Memento (2000). McNaughton's direction elevates what could have been simple exploitation into something more sophisticated, using the Florida setting's natural humidity and decay to create an atmosphere of moral corruption. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of the Erotic Thriller

The 1990s marked the commercial peak of the erotic thriller genre, with Wild Things arriving near the end of this golden age. Films like Fatal Attraction (1987) and Disclosure (1994) had established the commercial viability of combining psychological suspense with sexual content. However, as the millennium approached, the genre began moving from theatrical releases to cable and direct-to-video markets. Wild Things represents one of the last major studio investments in this genre, following a trajectory that began with Double Indemnity (1944) and continued through Body Double (1984).
